Nov 10, 2026

 Developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers can now try our latest frontier model. 

Koray Kavukcuoglu

SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google

Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning.

Two weeks ago, we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program. Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon, Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops.

Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. ...

signals.title: LangChain Deep Agents now natively supports Oracle AI Database 26ai and OCI Generative AI | ai-data-science
signals.excerpt:
AI agents can now take on whole tasks: plan the work, split it among specialists, run for minutes across dozens of steps, and hand back a finished result. LangChain’s open-source Deep Agents library packages that design. Teams building on Oracle want it where their data already lives: models on OCI Generative AI, knowledge and records in Oracle AI Database 26ai, and agent state kept in the same governed place.

That is now one call. Oracle’s open-source `langchain-oci` package natively supports LangChain Deep Agents: `create_deepagents_agent` connects the Deep Agents harness to OCI Generative AI models and to Oracle AI Database 26ai for search, memory, and state. Developers get planning, specialist sub-agents, a working filesystem, and human approval steps, on Oracle infrastructure, without writing the glue.

...

`langchain-oci` now includes `create_deepagents_agent`, available on PyPI with the `deepagents` extra:

```
pip install -U "langchain-oci[deepagents]"
```

One call returns a ready-to-run LangGraph agent that:

- Runs on OCI Generative AI, or on any tool-calling LangChain chat model you bring.
- Searches your data in Oracle AI Database 26ai. Point it at one or more stores and it generates three tools: `stats`, `search` (hybrid vector and keyword search, routed to the right store), and `get_document`. OpenSearch indices work the same way.
- Gets the full Deep Agents harness: a planning tool, sub-agents with their own context and tools, a virtual filesystem for notes and drafts, skills, structured output, and human-in-the-loop approval.
- Keeps its state in Oracle AI Database 26ai: thread checkpoints with `OracleSaver`, long-term memory with `OracleStore`, and durable files with `StoreBackend`, so a run can be inspected, resumed, or continued days later.

...

| Capability | Coverage |
| --- | --- |
| Models | OCI Generative AI chat models; any tool-calling LangChain chat model |
| Retrieval | Oracle AI Database 26ai (OracleVS and Oracle Text, hybrid) and OpenSearch, with automatic routing across stores |
| Agent harness | planning, sub-agents, virtual filesystem, skills, structured output, middleware |
| Human in the loop | approval before chosen tool calls |
| Persistence | `OracleSaver` checkpoints, `OracleStore` memory, `StoreBackend` files |

...

LangChain publishes this design as the open-source Deep Agents library, built on LangGraph (documentation, source).

signals.excerpt:
Meituan open-sourced LongCat-2.5 on November 10 under the MIT License. It supports commercial inference deployment and further training without additional authorization. The model targets long-horizon agent tasks and features a native multimodal architecture, with 1.6 trillion total parameters, about 48 billion parameters activated per token, and support for a one-million-token context. The weights are available on HuggingFace, with the technical blog and API platform also opened simultaneously.

...

Inference adopts the W4A4 scheme, quantizing expert weights and activations to 4-bit and executing them on native INT4 matrix multiplication units. FlatQuant is used to optimize MoE quantization accuracy, with downstream performance comparable to that before quantization, while dedicated fused operators help reduce costs. Both training and supervised fine-tuning use long-sequence training. Targeting domestic AI accelerators with less than 80GB of VRAM per card, it uses FSDP double sharding and hybrid vocabulary parallelism to distribute memory pressure. This configuration increases per-GPU throughput in long-sequence SFT by 86% over the DDP baseline, providing an efficiency foundation for open-source deployment of trillion-parameter MoE models.

signals.title: Start and Restore GPU Workloads in Seconds with NVIDIA Snapshot | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
NVIDIA Snapshot, a new open-source component of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform, makes initialized GPU workloads reusable across inference replicas—speeding startup and recovery.

When inference demand spikes or a replica fails, available GPUs don’t translate immediately into serving capacity. Initializing an LLM workload—a process known as a cold start—can take minutes, delaying scaling and recovery.

Snapshot is a checkpoint and restore system for GPU workloads on Kubernetes. It captures a fully initialized workload—including CPU and GPU memory—and restores that state on compatible infrastructure, bringing inference capacity online in seconds instead of minutes. Figure 1 shows the startup sequence. Snapshot skips repeated workload initialization; infrastructure provisioning and container image loading remain outside the measured restore path.

...

Design partners have also evaluated Snapshot on their own workloads:

- Crusoe, an upstream contributor to Snapshot, reduced GLM-5.3 Pod readiness time from roughly 8 minutes to 31 seconds on NVIDIA HGX B300.
- Saturn Cloud, a token factory platform, benchmarked NVIDIA Snapshot for scale-from-zero inference, cutting vLLM startup from 2–8.5 minutes to 6–34 seconds on NVIDIA HGX B300.

The following benchmarks show how Snapshot accelerates inference startup across vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM (TRT-LLM)—with models from 600 million parameters to mixture-of-experts (MoE) models with 1 TB checkpoints on 8 GPUs. Across all tested configurations, Snapshot brings a replica back in under 45 seconds, 8x to 36x faster than a cold start.

...

- GPU: NVIDIA B200

...

- Inference engines:

...

### Results

The benchmarks show four main findings.

- Restore times stayed under 43 seconds: Across all tested configurations, Snapshot restored replicas in 3.6 to 42.7 seconds—8x to 36x faster than cold start. The largest MoE models, with checkpoints of about 600 GB to 1 TB across eight GPUs, restored in under 43 seconds compared with cold-start times of 6 to 19 minutes.
- Restoring skips more than weight loading: Cold-start time includes loading weights, compiling and autotuning kernels, and capturing CUDA graphs. Snapshot restores the initialized workload, skipping these repeated steps.
- Checkpointing pays off with the first restored replica: In every tested configuration, checkpoint time plus restore time was shorter than a single cold start. Checkpoint creation took 15 seconds to 5.5 minutes, depending on the model and configuration.
- Moving GPU state dominates large restores: For the eight-GPU MoE configurations, restoring GPU state took 18 to 29 seconds. Restoring CPU process state with CRIU took 4.2 to 10.8 seconds.

signals.title: RagLeap v0.13.1 and ragleap-memory 0.3.0: Better Action Auditing and Optional Vector Search - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
# RagLeap v0.13.1 and ragleap-memory 0.3.0: Better Action Auditing and Optional Vector Search 

RagLeap has two new releases focused on an important part of building reliable AI systems: understanding what agents do and improving how they retrieve information.

- ragleap-core v0.13.1 introduces structured audit log lines for agent actions.
- ragleap-memory 0.3.0 adds optional vector and hybrid search using an embedder function supplied by the developer.

Both releases are open-source and designed for self-hosted environments.

...

## 2. ragleap-memory 0.3.0: Optional Vector and Hybrid Search 

The second release focuses on memory retrieval.

Ragleap Memory 0.3.0 adds vector and hybrid search while keeping keyword search as the default.

One design decision is particularly important: the library does not include provider-specific embedding code, API keys, or network access.

Developers supply their own embedder function.

This gives applications control over where embedding requests go and which embedding implementation they use.

### New search modes 

The library supports three search modes:

- `keyword` — the default and existing search behaviour.
- `vector` — cosine similarity over stored vectors.
- `hybrid` — combines keyword and vector results using reciprocal rank fusion.

Example: 

```
results = store.search(
    "relevant information",
    mode="hybrid",
    query_vector=query_vector,
)

```

The exact embedder and vector-generation workflow are controlled by the application.

...

### Security and limitations 

There are important limitations developers should understand:

- Stored vectors are currently unencrypted and may reveal information about the original text.
- Text sent to an embedder leaves the process wherever that embedder sends it.
- Vector search scans at most `max_vector_candidates` eligible entries.
- Retrieval quality depends on the selected embedder and has not yet been measured.
- No independent security review has been completed.

These limitations are documented in the library's threat model.

...

RagLeap is an open-source, self-hosted AI employee platform. We welcome developers, testers, technical writers, and contributors interested in building practical AI infrastructure.

signals.title:
What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
            
            
            - Google Developers Blog
signals.excerpt:
## TLDR

Today, we announce the General Availability of Pathways on Google Cloud Platform. In this post, you will learn about Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own large models, including Gemini. We discuss how Pathways addresses the coordination challenge by introducing one client that describes the whole computation as a graph, and how the distributed runtime places it, moves the tensors, and keeps the accelerators busy.

...

That is the idea behind Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own largest models, including Gemini. Pathways runs JAX programs on TPUs and it is available on Google Cloud.

...

With Pathways, you define the end-to-end computation from a single Python client, without writing custom coordination code, and a distributed runtime executes it. That client is decoupled from the hardware. It runs on an ordinary CPU machine and you write your program against virtual devices; a resource manager maps them onto real chips, and a worker on each accelerator host runs the compiled programs it receives.

...

Also, the same capability helps when a host fails or the hardware isn't ready yet. If a host dies, the resource manager remaps the work onto healthy chips and the run keeps going instead of relaunching the whole job, which is the basis for elastic training. And because the program targets virtual devices, compilation can start before the physical chips are provisioned, so setup overlaps with provisioning instead of waiting on it.

signals.title: Introducing TPU Sync: Fast KV cache & weight transfer on TPU | Google Cloud Blog
signals.excerpt:
Introducing TPU Sync: Fast KV cache and weight transfer for inference and RL on TPU

November 9, 2026

...

As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers to rollout samplers during RL. Whenever this state is trapped inside a single chip's memory or stalled on network transfers, AI accelerators sit idle.

We designed TPU Sync from first principles to serve as the model-state layer across TPU clusters — built on the architectural insight that accelerator High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network (DCN) should operate as a single, co-designed memory hierarchy. An open-source, native C++ library, TPU Sync moves TPU-tiled tensors directly across this hierarchy with asynchronous DMA transfers that overlap data movement with active computation.

For inference, it decouples TPU compute from network backpressure and turns host DRAM, local SSDs, and Google Cloud Managed Lustre into an automated, multi-tier KV cache; and for RL, it exposes low-level DMA and DCN primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to stream updated weights from trainers to samplers. By accessing device buffers in place rather than copying or locking them, TPU Sync consistently slashes KV transfer latency by over 90% and reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) by an average of 90% for heavyweight open-weight MoE models (235B–480B parameters) in prefix-caching and disaggregated-serving workloads, compared to running without TPU Sync.

...

- Long-context AI agents and multi-turn chats: When interacting with an AI agent over an extended 256K to 1M+ token session or analyzing massive documents, the model generates a continuously growing KV cache. Instead of allowing this state to exhaust HBM capacity, TPU Sync automatically tiers older KV blocks out of TPU HBM and into large pools of host RAM (with experimental tiering to shared secondary storage).
- Enterprise applications with heavy system prompts (prefix caching): AI serving platforms receive thousands of queries that share common instructions or documents. Rather than recomputing prefixes that the model has already processed, TPU Sync extends the prefix cache into distributed host memory so concurrent sessions can reuse precomputed KV blocks and bypass redundant prefill computation.
- Disaggregated serving architecture (prefill/decode): In modern enterprise deployments, workloads are isolated: Compute-bound nodes process the initial massive prompt (prefill), while memory-bound nodes draft the response token-by-token (decode). TPU Sync bridges this hardware gap by acting as a high-bandwidth Host-to-Host (H2H) streaming pipeline. It routes the processed context directly from the prefill nodes to the decode nodes, consistently delivering an over 90% reduction in data transfer overhead.
- Reinforcement learning pipelines (experimental): Validated on internal RL workloads and included in the repository as an experimental module, TPU Sync provides low-level DMA and DCN transfer primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to synchronize model weights between trainers and inference samplers — including automatic resharding across different trainer and sampler parallelism layouts — to reduce the time rollout workers spend waiting on weight updates.

...

- Over 90% KV transfer overhead cut: For heavyweight models like Qwen3 235B, median KV transfer latency dropped from several seconds down to a flat ~230 ms.
- Substantial TTFT reduction: Demonstrated an average of 60% reduction in TTFT for heavyweight models (Qwen3 235B) under controlled, low-concurrency testing benchmarks, and an average of 90% for 480B under low concurrency.
- Substantial high-traffic scalability: During sustained traffic spikes, TPU Sync achieves an average of 30% to 70% increase in token output throughput for 235B, depending on traffic distribution.

...

TPU Sync is available today as open source with Python wheels for both PyTorch (`tpu-sync-torch`) and JAX (`tpu-sync-jax`), and is integrated with vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, and llm-d on GKE. Visit the GitHub repository to explore the architecture docs, C++ and Python APIs, and deployment guides.

signals.title: Cloud Pathways, a distributed ML runtime, is GA | Google Cloud Blog
signals.excerpt:
November 9, 2026

##### Shaurya Gupta

Software Engineer, Google

##### Monica Song

Product Manager, Google

Today, we are thrilled to announce the general availability (GA) of Cloud Pathways (Pathways on Cloud) on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) as a core runtime pillar of the Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer.

Originally engineered by Google DeepMind to train and serve Google's frontier models — including Gemini — Pathways is our distributed machine-learning runtime designed for massive, heterogeneous accelerator fleets. In fact, over the last 90 days alone, leading AI companies and global enterprises have processed more than 130 million Cloud TPU chip-hours using Pathways on GKE, across a broad range of TPU generations.

With Cloud Pathways, every Google Cloud customer can use the same single-controller runtime, colocated Python sidecars, and elastic fault tolerance that power Google's largest AI workloads. We are also pleased to announce a Preview integration with Cluster Director to extend Cloud Pathways to Slurm clusters, supporting unified multi-slice JAX execution, elastic training, and interactive notebooks.

...

Cloud Pathways has the following features:

- Single-controller orchestration: In Cloud Pathways, a single controller manages graph evaluation, persistent Cloud Storage compilation caching, and asynchronous XLA HLO dispatch across TPU slices.
- Colocated Python sidecars: Client-side colocated Python sidecar containers (with shared-memory support) let you run compute-intensive Python logic such as distributed data loading and checkpointing directly on TPU hosts.
- Resilient and elastic training: Cloud Pathways decouples job survival from individual slice interruptions with elastic training (`pathwaysutils`) using host-memory snapshots to dynamically reshard training down to N-1 slices during hardware failures without crashing the client.
- Interactive mode and Shared Pathways Service: Run, inspect, and debug JAX workloads interactively from a notebook or terminal using interactive mode, or share a long-running pool of Cloud TPU slices on demand across multiple users and jobs with the Shared Pathways Service.

...

Cloud Pathways is generally available today in all Google Cloud regions supporting Cloud TPU v5e, TPU v5p, Trillium (TPU v6e), and Ironwood (TPU 7x) on GKE, with versioned container images (`us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways`) supporting JAX `0.10.1+`. Cloud Pathways is also available in Preview on Slurm TPU clusters in Cluster Director.

I read their source code, followed agent-memory research, reported issues, and contributed pull requests. Some were merged. My target is state-of-the-art accuracy with disciplined token use and less irrelevant context. I care about the tokens needed to build memory as well as those supplied to the agent when it answers.

...

This helped clarify the boundary I want between memory and the agent’s ReAct loop. Memory should return relevant, source-backed evidence within a reasonable token and latency budget. The agent decides whether it needs to investigate further, makes targeted follow-up searches, and reasons from the sources. Explicit reasons can remain searchable in the evidence without requiring a separate causal graph.

That is the contribution I hope OAM can make to research and practical use: reproducible findings about which mechanisms help, alongside a complete open-source implementation that developers can run, inspect, modify, and improve.

signals.title: Intel Day-0 Support for Muse Spark Open [2026]
signals.excerpt:
Intel Corporation said on October 15, 2026 that it had enabled “day-0 support” for Meta’s 816-billion-parameter debut of Muse Spark Open, meaning the chipmaker’s hardware could run the model the moment Meta flipped the switch rather than weeks or months later. According to Intel’s newsroom announcement, the company enabled the open-weight, multimodal mixture-of-experts model across both Intel Xeon processors and the still-unreleased Intel GPU D-series, using low-bit quantization to shrink the model’s footprint enough to fit on four accelerator cards. It is a narrow technical disclosure on its face, but it says a lot about where Intel is trying to plant its flag in a data center AI market it has mostly watched from the sidelines.

...

Intel’s announcement is specific about mechanism, if sparse on the kind of marketing superlatives chipmakers usually reach for. The company says it enabled support across Intel Xeon processors and Intel GPU D-series platforms “through targeted low-bit model quantization,” according to Intel’s own post. That phrase matters because Muse Spark Open was not designed with Intel silicon in mind by default; Meta’s launch-day verified hardware list, per its documentation, names Nvidia, AMD, Intel, and Apple as the platforms confirmed to run the model at release. Getting onto that list on day one required Intel to do the quantization work ahead of the public launch, not after it.

Intel also says Muse Spark Open “has been tested and is running on the upcoming Intel GPU D-series, today,” a notable claim given that GPU D-series has not formally shipped, one early coverage of the launch also flagged as unusual for a pre-release product. The demonstration Intel points to used four Intel GPU D-series GPUs working together, each carrying 160 GB of memory, for a combined 640 GB of addressable GPU memory across the cluster. That is the number doing the real work in this announcement: a single Intel GPU D-series card has more onboard memory than most training-era accelerators from any vendor, and four of them stacked together is enough headroom to hold an 816-billion-parameter model’s weights with room to spare for inference overhead.

...

Intel’s day-0 support rests on two separate quantization paths, each tuned for a different piece of its hardware lineup. According to Intel’s announcement, the MXFP4 weights, delivered in compressed-tensors format, are built to use native hardware acceleration on Intel GPU D-series GPUs. Separately, INT4 weights in GPTQ format are aimed at Xeon processors running in weight-only quantization mode, a configuration Intel says is chosen specifically “to minimize memory footprint and latency.”

The distinction is not cosmetic. MXFP4 is a floating-point-style low-bit format that plays to the strengths of dedicated matrix-math hardware, which is exactly what Intel built into GPU D-series in the form of its XMX engines. INT4 weight-only quantization, by contrast, keeps computation in a format that a general-purpose CPU can execute efficiently without specialized tensor cores, at the cost of needing more careful calibration to avoid accuracy loss. Running both paths at once is how Intel is positioning Muse Spark Open as deployable whether a customer has GPU D-series hardware on hand or is stuck, for now, with Xeon-only infrastructure.

# Unsloth Boosts Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Efficiency with New Dynamic V3.1 GGUF Quantizations

Unsloth has launched Dynamic v3.1 GGUF quantizations for the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model. This update improves accuracy by up to 15% and increases inference speed while optimizing memory usage for local deployment.

...

## Unsloth Releases Dynamic V3.1 GGUFs for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next

Unsloth has released its new Dynamic v3.1 GGUF quantizations for the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model, according to the developer's announcement. This update introduces significant improvements in accuracy and inference efficiency for local deployment of large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models.

The release is technically significant because it optimizes the 125B parameter Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model—which features 6B activated parameters and a 256K context window—for memory-constrained environments as detailed in the Hugging Face repository. By utilizing the Dynamic v3.1 algorithm, these quants aim to maintain high reasoning capabilities while reducing the computational overhead typically associated with frontier-scale models.

...

The update introduces several key technical advancements:

- Engram Switching: A new process allows users to "mix and match" engram components across different precisions, such as BF16, Q8 0, Q5 1, and IQ4_NL as described in the Unsloth documentation. This enables developers to swap table shards to optimize the balance between disk space and precision.
- Precision Metrics: The relative Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) compared to BF16 is notably low across formats: 0.0053 for Q8 0, 0.0376 for Q5 1, and 0.0757 for IQ4_NL according to the technical specifications.
- Hardware Scaling: The model's requirements scale based on quantization, ranging from 32GB of RAM for the smallest 1-bit version to 355GB for BF16 as noted in the Unsloth usage guide.

## Performance Results

The Dynamic v3.1 quants demonstrate superior performance compared to previous GSQ-RCO versions and other frontier quants of similar size as reported in the Unsloth technical notes:

- Accuracy: A 10-15% increase in accuracy on benchmarks including DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, and Aider Polyglot.
- Efficiency: Up to 50% reduction in token usage and a 7% increase in inference speed as documented in the Hugging Face release notes.
- Benchmark Validation: Results were verified through 26.2B tokens of benchmarking, including 18.1B tokens for DeepSWE and 5.2B for Terminal Bench.

...

The new GGUF files are currently available for download via the Unsloth Hugging Face repository.

signals.title: Meituan open-sources LongCat-2.5: 1.6T params, MIT licence
signals.excerpt:
Meituan's LongCat team released the full weights of LongCat-2.5 under the MIT licence, making a frontier-class multimodal model free to download, fine-tune and resell — no usage caps, no revenue thresholds, no request for permission. The model went live as a hosted API on November 2; what changed overnight is that anyone with the hardware can now run it themselves. Alongside the main checkpoint, Meituan published a W4A4 quantised build and deployment notes for domestic Chinese accelerators, per the model card on Hugging Face.

LongCat-2.5 is a native multimodal mixture-of-experts model: 1.6 trillion total parameters, roughly 48 billion activated per token, and a 1-million-token context window. Meituan built it for long-horizon agentic work rather than chat — complex codebase development, full-project builds, visual programming that produces interactive 3D scenes, and business analysis spreadsheets. The model card lists the design bets plainly: native-resolution images converted into discrete tokens and trained jointly with text, long-horizon reinforcement learning on real engineering tasks and reproduced agent failures, and multi-teacher distillation from specialised agent, reasoning and interaction models.

...

The benchmark table is impressive and narrower than the headline number suggests. Across 31 evaluations and nine comparison models — including Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6-Sol, GLM-5.3, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash — LongCat-2.5 finishes first on four: BrowseComp at 91.9, ALE v1.1 at 38.5, ResearchRubrics at 81.0 and 3DCodeBench at 55.4. Two of those wins are photo finishes. BrowseComp is 91.9 against DeepSeek's 91.5 and Kimi K3's 91.2; ResearchRubrics is 81.0 against DeepSeek's 80.9. The other two are real gaps: ALE puts it 3.3 points clear of Kimi and 8.2 ahead of GPT-5.5, and 3DCodeBench — generating 3D code from a text prompt — is 1.1 points ahead of Claude Opus 5 and the only category where a Chinese model leads at all.

The losses are just as instructive. On Terminal Bench v4.0, the hardest agentic terminal test in the table, LongCat-2.5 scores 38.5 against Claude Opus 5's 53.9 — a 15-point gap that no amount of BrowseComp leadership offsets. It trails DeepSeek on DeepSWE (64.6 versus 74.2), on AutomationBench (51.8 versus 54.8) and on JobBench (65.4 versus Claude Opus 5's 66.7). On Terminal Bench v2.1 the two leaders are effectively tied, 88.4 to 89.1, which makes the v4.0 spread the more interesting number: the new benchmark separates models that the old one could not.

...

The engineering notes are aimed squarely at the constraint Western labs do not have. Meituan trained and serves LongCat-2.5 on domestic AI accelerators with under 80 GB of memory per card, sharding parameters and expert exchange across supernodes and overlapping communication with compute; its long-sequence fine-tuning configuration reports 86% higher per-device throughput than a standard distributed baseline. The W4A4 build quantises expert weights and activations to four bits and, against an INT8 baseline, lifts prefill throughput 43.3% and decode throughput 42.77% while cutting time-to-first-token 15.9% and time-per-output-token 19.7%. Squeezing a 1.6T model onto export-controlled silicon is the strategic problem Chinese labs are actually solving, and this release documents the solution in public.

signals.title: Agent memory is eating GraphRAG's lunch, and rerankers just got a lot cheaper
signals.excerpt:
This digest covers RAG and GraphRAG developments from 2026-10-19 through 2026-11-09: new retrieval and reranking papers from arXiv and Hugging Face Daily Papers, agent-memory architecture writeups from Anthropic and LangChain, document-parsing and graph-tooling updates from LlamaIndex and Neo4j, and a production deep-dive from Latent Space.

## 🔥 Highlights 

1. The components of agent memory — Anthropic's own layered memory architecture, with data on when curation beats raw search. 
2. Building Evidence-Grounded Agent Memory with OpenWiki and Graphs — a graph layer beats a wiki alone, without full GraphRAG overhead.
3. Agentic GraphRAG and an explorer for your own stack — a runnable reference agent over a real knowledge graph, published today. 
4. Re³Rank: Listwise Reranking with Reasoning-Conditioned Retrieval Heads — a 0.6B reranker beating 32B models, straight cost win.
5. RAGCompass: Generalizable Retriever Routing via Reranking — a trainable router for picking the right retriever per query.

...

- ArcRAG: Agentic Compositional Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs — 2026-11-04. Builds a query-specific view of a knowledge graph at inference time from the entities named in the question, then plans and repairs multi-hop traversals as Cypher queries. Practical value: a construction-agnostic retriever that works whether your graph came from a schema-guided or an open-extraction pipeline.
- Typed-Centrality Grounding for Agentic GraphRAG: A Symbolic Approach for Agentic Reasoning — 2026-11-06. Computes centrality measures per entity type as a deterministic symbolic signal alongside text-similarity retrieval, targeting GraphRAG's habit of treating the graph as homogeneous. Reports more context-consistent answers on a real-world dataset — useful if your GraphRAG hallucinates relationships that pure text similarity misses.
- QueryFlow: Multi-Hop Graph Retrieval with Adaptive Query Evolution — 2026-11-03. Updates the query representation during multi-hop traversal by folding query-conditioned graph summaries back into a shared query state. Reports double-digit gains on macro Recall@10 and LLM-Acc across four multi-hop QA datasets, addressing evidence that only becomes relevant after intermediate hops.
- RAGCompass: Generalizable Retriever Routing via Reranking — 2026-11-03. Scores retrieved passages themselves to pick the best retriever per query, trained contrastively against the answers each passage set produces. Reports a 28% relative F1 gain over the best single retriever, holding up on unseen corpora/retrievers — a generalizable routing layer for teams running multiple indexes.
- Re³Rank: Listwise Reranking with Reasoning-Conditioned Retrieval Heads — 2026-11-02. A listwise reranker where a generator writes a reasoning trace first, then a scorer uses that trace to produce relevance scores. Beats 11 baselines across 9 benchmarks, with a 0.6B variant outperforming 32B rerankers — a serious latency/cost lever for production rerank stages.
- DecisionRank: On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers — 2026-10-30. Distills a generative reranker's ranking knowledge into a non-autoregressive "decision model" via on-policy, item-space distillation. The 8B version matches its generative counterpart while running 16-25x faster.
- Retrieving from Your Own Mistakes: On-Policy Training of Embedding Models for Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation — 2026-10-29. Trains multi-hop retrievers on their own retrieval trajectories, including mistakes, labeling each visited state with the earliest missing gold passage. Improves evidence completeness on harder, out-of-distribution long-chain variants of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA.
- Reliability Stress Testing of RAG Retrieval under Query-Relevant Corpus Poisoning — 2026-11-03. Stress-tests the retrieval admission step against poisoned documents, showing query-tailored poison can fully compromise a dense retriever like BGE-small. Also evaluates overlap-based admission and MMR as mitigations — a concrete checklist for RAG exposed to untrusted corpora.
- MEMOIR: A Training-Free Memory Lifecycle for Long-Horizon LLM Agents — 2026-11-05. Combines judge-gated consolidation with retrospective attribution that credits memories that actually supported past answers, plus an exploration bonus for under-used memories. Targets two real production pains directly — consolidation discarding needed evidence, and retrieval favoring stale memories — with no added LLM calls on the write path.
- Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy — 2026-10-19. Shows that when long tool outputs are saved to files and retrieved on demand, GPT-5.1/5.2 lose 7.9-11.3 accuracy points via "evidence substitution" (answering from prior output instead of the retrieved file), while Claude models show no detectable cost. Explicitly flagging the authoritative output recovers most of the gap — a model-specific warning for agentic retrieval over tool/file outputs.
- Signed but Steerable: Measuring and Closing the Text-Vector Integrity Gap in Offline Retrieval-Augmented Generation — 2026-11-04. Shows that signed, precomputed embedding packs for offline/edge RAG only prove publisher identity, not that vectors match the text — cosine-tolerance checks and compressed-FAISS audits both fail to catch tampering. Proposes verifying quantization codes with a calibrated guard band, which caught attackers in testing — important if you ship or consume precomputed vector indexes.

signals.title: Changing how we measure AI chip inference performance | Epoch AI
signals.excerpt:
Inference performance improvements can be much larger than changes in raw compute speed (FLOP/s) suggest. We estimate that the Nvidia GB300 provides about 25× Nvidia H100’s inference capacity per chip on the agentic inference workloads we model, with only 2.5× the 8-bit FLOP per second.

Comparing FLOP/s alone would therefore underestimate GB300’s inference capacity relative to H100 by a factor of ten. This is because memory and inter-chip communication can matter more than arithmetic throughput for inference performance.

We introduce the Inference Performance Index (IPI) to capture these differences. The index compares how many requests each chip can serve at once across a range of required output speeds. IPI Version 1 focuses on agentic workloads and combines results across four representative models.

Scores are expressed in GB300 equivalents (GB300e), with GB300 scoring one by definition. 1 A score of two means we estimate that a chip can serve twice as many users or agents at once as GB300, on average across the workloads and output-speed requirements in the index. We use GB300 as our reference because it is a widely used inference GPU with leading benchmark performance, such as in SemiAnalysis InferenceX.

signals.excerpt:
LongCat 2.5 is Meituan's multimodal model, with 1.6 trillion total parameters and roughly 48 billion active for each token, and its weights can now be downloaded from Hugging Face under an MIT license. Compared with LongCat 2.0 it adds native vision and much heavier agentic training, though every benchmark in the release is reported by the vendor itself.

...

| Benchmark | LongCat 2.0 | LongCat 2.5 | Claude Opus 5 | GPT-5.6-Sol |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Terminal Bench v2.1 | 70.8 | 88.4 | 89.1* | 88.8* |
| Terminal Bench v4.0 | 3.0 | 38.5 | 53.9* | 37.3* |
| DeepSWE v1.1 | 9.7 | 64.6 | 68.8* | 72.7* |
| Program Bench | 2.5 | 25.5 | 37.0* | 23.0* |
| BrowseComp | 79.9 | 91.9 | 90.8* | 90.4* |
| HLE (with tools) | 37.5 | 63.1 | 64.7* | 58.0* |
| MCP Atlas | 61.8 | 83.1 | 85.8* | 81.8* |

The leap in DeepSWE, from 9.7 to 64.6, is the figure that stands out most. Terminal Bench v4.0 tells the same story, with a 3.0 turning into 38.5. These are the tests closest to a programmer's real work (fixing bugs in real repositories, getting around a terminal), and version 2.0 had fallen well behind on them.

...

For almost everyone the practical answer is no. The repository holds 208 files in BF16 format and takes up about 3.56 terabytes, which means a cluster of servers with memory for a trillion and a half parameters, not a workstation. The weight index even records 1.78 trillion parameters, more than the 1.6 declared (the gap probably comes from the embedding tables, which the card does not count).

On the hardware front the model card keeps its feet on the ground. It explains how to deploy the model only on NPUs (accelerators built for AI, made in China) through SGLang-FluentLLM and cites no instructions for Nvidia GPUs. The config.json file describes 38 layers, 768 routed experts with 12 active per token, 128 "zero-cost" experts and MLA-type attention (which compresses the context memory), with a maximum window of 524,288 positions. The benchmark notes, by contrast, talk about runs up to 1 million tokens, so anyone planning to use it on long contexts should check which of the two numbers applies in their own case.

...

On the infrastructure side the numbers all come from Meituan. Long training runs on accelerators with less than 80 GB of memory each, and the company reports per-device throughput 86% higher than a DDP baseline for its long sequences. W4A4 quantization (4-bit weights and activations) delivers, compared with a W8A8 setup, 43.3% more throughput in prefill and 42.77% in decoding, and with an 8-bit KV cache decoding rises by 92%. The chip maker is never named.

signals.title: Railtown AI Launches Open-Source Railtracks Swift RAG Framework for Private On-Device AI Agents on Apple Devices
signals.excerpt:
Railtown AI Technologies Inc. (CSE: RAIL) (OTCQB: RLAIF) has announced the availability of Railtracks Swift RAG, an open-source library within its Railtracks Swift Agent Development Kit, enabling developers to build privacy-focused AI applications on Apple devices. The library allows documents to be transformed into searchable knowledge bases stored locally on a user's device, with AI retrieval and response generation occurring without transmitting data to cloud services. The release builds on the company's October 21, 2026, launch of its Railtracks Swift ADK and extends Railtown's open-source developer ecosystem into Apple's native Swift development environment. Investors may be watching how this strategy drives adoption of Railtown's commercial Conductr platform over time.

...

Railtracks Swift RAG allows developers to ingest PDF, text, CSV and JSON files and organise their contents into structured, searchable passages stored on a user's Apple device. Using a process known as Retrieval-Augmented Generation, applications can retrieve relevant passages and supply them to a language model to generate responses grounded in the user's own documents. When configured with Apple's supported on-device AI capabilities, the entire knowledge retrieval and response-generation workflow can operate locally, without transmitting documents or queries to a remote AI provider. Retrieved passages retain references to their original source materials, allowing developers to surface the basis for a generated response.

...

A key feature of the library is its support for fully local AI configurations, where document processing, embedding, storage and response generation remain on the user's device. The library also supports cloud-based and hybrid embedding approaches, giving developers flexibility to choose architectures suited to their applications. Additionally, Railtracks Swift RAG includes a native Core Spotlight pipeline that developers can combine with Apple's App Intents and Shortcuts frameworks to expose knowledge-search functionality through Siri. Railtown notes that Siri interactions may involve processing through Apple services, and that fully local processing applies specifically to the application's configured knowledge base and AI workflow.

...

Railtracks Swift RAG is available under an MIT licence within Railtown's Railtracks Swift repository, allowing developers to use, modify and incorporate the library without a commercial licence. The company states it views developer engagement as an important component of its long-term commercialisation strategy, believing that developers building increasingly sophisticated applications may subsequently require the deployment, orchestration and observability capabilities available through its Conductr platform. The immediate share price impact was not clear from available public information.

signals.title: LowRAM Claims 26.9× KV Cache Compression at Test Time | AI Weekly
signals.excerpt:
## TL;DR

- LowRAM reports 26.9× KV cache compression at 94.5% of baseline performance on long contexts when stacked with quantisation and eviction.
- The method fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time that reconstructs values from keys, storing residuals only for the worst-reconstructed tokens.
- At 4× compression the authors claim near-lossless behaviour across three model families and up to 5× higher peak decode throughput.

...

LowRAM, a new test-time method for shrinking the KV cache, reports 26.9× compression at 94.5% of baseline performance on long contexts, according to a preprint posted to arXiv.

The approach treats keys and values asymmetrically. Authors Teresa Delgado, Hugo Hazard, Martin Benfeghoul, Jun Wang and Zafeirios Fountas identify what they call a complementary axis: "within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys." They fit a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and store residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, which the paper describes as giving "4× near-lossless value compression." That is paired with cross-layer low-rank key compression.

LowRAM, the paper says, "stays close to lossless across three model families" at 4× compression, and can reach "up to 5× higher peak decode throughput" at that same ratio. The 26.9× headline figure is reached only when the method is stacked on top of quantisation and eviction, which the authors position as composable rather than competing techniques.

signals.title: Runpod launches batch inference for cheaper AI workloads
signals.excerpt:
Mon, 9th Nov 2026 (Yesterday) 

 KAREN JOY BACUDO Finance Editor 

Runpod has launched Batch Inference on its serverless platform for non-urgent AI workloads.

The product lets developers send background jobs to the same inference endpoints and model weights they already use for live traffic, rather than building a separate setup for offline processing. The aim is to keep heavy tasks away from the interactive requests handled by real-time applications.

Background tasks can include scoring benchmark datasets, embedding large document collections and evaluating AI models. The jobs run on dedicated batch workers, so they do not use the concurrency limits reserved for live user requests.

Developers can submit batches of up to 5,000 JSON requests through an API call or by pasting raw JSON into a web console. Endpoints can support up to 10 active batches and 50,000 queued requests at once, while larger enterprise configurations can handle up to one million requests a day.

Runpod is also pitching the launch on cost. Batch compute is priced at a 30% discount to standard GPUs and at a 20% discount to higher-end Nvidia hardware, including the H100, H200, B200 and B300.

Jobs are scheduled on off-peak capacity, with multi-hour start times and a best-effort completion target within 24 hours. That makes the service suited to workloads that can tolerate delays in exchange for lower compute spending.

...

Runpod said more than one million developers use its cloud platform. It offers infrastructure for different stages of AI development, including experimentation, training, fine-tuning, deployment and scaling.

signals.title: AWS Adds Single-Shot RAG to Amazon Bedrock — AI In Context
signals.excerpt:
AWS's November 9, 2026 update lets Bedrock users pick retrieval-only, single-shot RAG, or multi-step agentic retrieval via one parameter — trading model calls for answer depth.

...

- On November 9, 2026, AWS added single-shot RAG and retrieval-only requests to Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base via AgenticRetrieveStream.
- The maxAgentIteration parameter now spans 0–5: 0 returns passages only, 1 retrieves once and generates an answer, 2–5 keep agentic behavior.
- Agentic retrieval supports up to five retrievers per request, and every mode supports multiple knowledge bases.
- AWS supplies no measured latency or cost comparisons and recommends customers benchmark on their own knowledge bases.
- Retrieval-only mode returns passages without score or location fields, unlike the separate Retrieve API.

Amazon Web Services announced on November 9, 2026 that Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports single-shot retrieval-augmented generation (RAG — a pattern that fetches source passages and feeds them to a model to ground its answer) and passage-only requests through the AgenticRetrieveStream API. An expanded 0–5 range for the maxAgentIteration parameter lets applications choose source retrieval only, a one-search answer, or the service's existing multi-step agentic retrieval.

...

The values map cleanly onto three behaviors, according to AWS:

- 0 returns matching passages without generating an answer.
- 1 retrieves once and generates an answer when generateResponse=true is set.
- 2 through 5 preserve the existing agentic behavior, with iterative planning and retrieval.

Every mode supports multiple knowledge bases. AWS stresses that "single-shot" refers to one retrieval, not a restriction to one knowledge base.

Single-shot RAG uses one foundation-model call for generation. Retrieval-only requests use none. AWS says single-shot operation can reduce latency and model usage relative to agentic retrieval — but the announcement supplies no measured latency or cost comparison. Enterprises will need to benchmark on their own corpora.

signals.title: NVIDIA Releases Dynamo-Optimized Recipes for Four Korean Open Models | ZICQ
signals.excerpt:
Summary: NVIDIA has released Dynamo-optimized deployment recipes for A.X K2, K-EXAONE 2.0, Solar Open 2, and Motif-3. Targeted at NVIDIA B200 deployments, the recipes provide reproducible configurations for multi-node inference, including model sharding, request routing, and inter-GPU communication. NVIDIA claims up to 2× out-of-the-box performance, but the figure is vendor-reported and requires independent validation under clearly defined throughput, latency, concurrency, and cost conditions.

...

NVIDIA has published four deployment recipes optimized with Dynamo, its open-source distributed inference-serving framework. They cover A.X K2 from SK Telecom, K-EXAONE 2.0 from LG AI Research, Solar Open 2 from Upstage, and Motif-3 from Motif Technologies.

The configurations target production inference on NVIDIA B200 GPUs in multi-node environments. Their main purpose is not to introduce new model architectures, but to package model sharding, request routing, and inter-GPU communication into reproducible deployment baselines. NVIDIA claims that the recipes can deliver up to 2× performance out of the box compared with the relevant baseline configurations.

The practical significance is straightforward: downloadable open weights do not automatically imply economical production deployment. Once a model exceeds the memory capacity of one GPU, tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, and potentially expert parallelism introduce synchronization, scheduling, and load-balancing costs that can materially change throughput and latency.

...

Dynamo is a distributed inference-serving framework designed for data-center-scale ... It separates request handling from model execution and coordinates model state across GPU nodes.

...

Dynamo addresses this at three levels:

1. Model sharding: It assigns parameters and computation across multiple GPUs so that the model no longer has to fit in a single device.
2. Request routing: It directs requests to suitable execution workers, improving load balance and reducing queueing.
3. Communication coordination: It manages data movement between nodes and avoids inefficient synchronization paths on every decoding step.

...

NVIDIA's “up to 2×” figure should be treated as an upper bound under specific model, hardware, and baseline conditions rather than a guaranteed multiplier for every deployment. Multi-node inference performance depends on at least six factors:

- Intra-node versus inter-node bandwidth: High-bandwidth NVLink domains remain within a server, but traffic crossing nodes still depends on InfiniBand, RoCE, and topology quality.

...

Production checks should also verify whether each recipe pins a specific model revision and weight format, whether quantization causes unacceptable output drift, and whether node failures, autoscaling, and request retries remain safe and idempotent. Operators must also confirm license compatibility, security isolation, data-residency requirements, and end-to-end traceability when converting public checkpoints into production images.
